title: Comprehensive Genomic Analysis of Patients With Non–Small-Cell Lung Cancer Using Blood-Based Circulating Tumor DNA Assay: Findings From the BFAST Database of a Single Center in Taiwan
author: Hsin-Yi Wang; Chao-Chi Ho; Yen-Ting Lin; Wei-Yu Liao; Chung-Yu Chen; Jin-Yuan Shih; Chong-Jen Yu
text:
Abstract
PURPOSE
The Blood First Assay Screening Trial (BFAST) is a prospective study using next-generation sequencing (NGS) of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in treatment-naïve advanced/metastatic non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We compared liquid biopsy to tissue testing and analyzed genomic alterations in Taiwanese patients with NSCLC using the BFAST database.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
A total of 269 patients underwent FoundationOne Liquid Companion Diagnostic (F1LCDx) assay at the National Taiwan University Hospital, of whom 264 underwent tissue-based genetic testing also. We analyzed the actionable mutations and the concordance between tissue-based genetic testing, which was limited to EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and BRAF, in a real-life clinical setting and blood-based NGS in the clinical trial. Additionally, we analyzed the co-occurring genomic alterations from the blood-based ctDNA assay.
RESULTS
A total of 76.2% patients showed actionable mutations. Standard tissue testing did not detect known driver alterations in about 22.7% of the patients (sensitivity, 70.24%). Liquid NGS detected additional mutations (RET, KRAS, MET, and ErbB2) in 14% of the patients, which went undetected by the standard-of-care testing. The complementary use of ctDNA NGS increased the detection rate by 42%. The F1LCDx assay had a sensitivity of 83.41%. Lower tumor and metastasis stages predicted nondetected blood-based NGS ctDNA results. Common co-occurring mutations in the blood-based NGS ctDNA assay were TP53, DNMT3A, TET2, PIK3CA, CTNNB1, and RB1. Among the patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC, TET2 co-occurring alterations correlated with shorter progression-free survival of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment.
CONCLUSION
NGS ctDNA analysis in comprehensive genetic testing improves actionable mutation identification, vital for treating Asian NSCLC cases with high actionable mutation rates. Lower stages correlated with undetected blood-based NGS ctDNA assay results.
Genomic analysis using a blood-based ctDNA assay enhances actionable mutation detection.
INTRODUCTION
The landscape of non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treatment shifted with successful targeted therapies. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines recommend broad molecular testing for lung cancer treatment to identify patients who would benefit from targeted therapies. However, obtaining adequate tissue biopsy specimens for NSCLC is becoming increasingly challenging owing to the growing number of biomarkers, resulting in inadequate samples for comprehensive molecular analysis.1 Besides, on the basis of the tumor location and patient's clinical condition, tissue collection can be challenging or time-consuming. The limitations of tissue-based testing can be overcome by blood-based next-generation sequencing (NGS). Multiple studies have confirmed the feasibility of NSCLC mutation detection using plasma-based circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) NGS.1-3 However, liquid biopsy also reportedly possesses limitations in situations where tumors have low ctDNA shedding, low extrathoracic metastatic spread, or solitary involvement of sanctuary sites.4,5
CONTEXT
Key Objective
The Blood First Assay Screening Trial (BFAST) is a prospective study, screening for actionable genetic alterations using next-generation sequencing (NGS) of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). We compared liquid biopsy to tissue testing and analyzed genomic alterations in Taiwanese patients with non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) at a single center using the BFAST database.
Knowledge Generated
Clinically relevant actionable mutations were identified in 76% patients after comprehensive genetic profiling by both clinical tissue and liquid testing. The complementary use of ctDNA NGS testing increased the actionable mutation detection rate. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)–mutated NSCLC, co-occurring genomic alterations in TET2 were associated with shorter progression-free survival of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors treatment.
Relevance
Our results underscore the vital importance of conducting thorough molecular assessments, especially given the escalating adoption of targeted therapies. Lower stages were linked to undetectable results in the blood-based NGS ctDNA assay.
The Blood First Assay Screening Trial (BFAST) is a prospective study that evaluated the clinical activity of targeted therapies or immunotherapy in treatment-naïve advanced/metastatic NSCLC. These patients were screened for actionable genetic alterations using NGS of ctDNA.6 The National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) is one of the study sites for BFAST, and the blood-based NGS assay provided genomic alteration results for the enrolled patients. Our study aimed to assess the effectiveness of liquid biopsy versus standard tissue testing and analyzed the correlation between clinical outcomes and co-occurring mutations identified through comprehensive molecular analysis.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study Design and Patients
Written informed consent was obtained from all patients for initial blood screening. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of NTUH (202304030RINA). An additional retrospective analysis of the BFAST screening cohort in Taiwan was conducted. BFAST (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03178552) is an ongoing phase II/III, global, multicenter, open-label, multicohort study. The enrolled patients were age 18 years and older and had untreated unresectable stage IIIB not amenable to concurrent chemoradiation treatment or stage IV metastatic NSCLC.
A total of 269 patients underwent FoundationOne Liquid Companion Diagnostic (F1LCDx) screening for the BFAST between February 2019 and March 2022 at NTUH; 41 of them joined the BFAST natural history cohort. Global BFAST analysis and natural history cohort analysis are ongoing but do not affect our study's outcomes. We retrospectively used NTUH BFAST enrollees as our study cohort. Genomic alterations obtained from the blood-based NGS assay were available from the BFAST study group. The clinical characteristics, outcomes, and tissue-based genetic testing results were obtained from the medical records. All the patients underwent comprehensive genetic testing, including blood-based NGS and standard-of-care tissue EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and BRAF single gene testing. Tissue NGS was optional, on the basis of the clinician's and patient's decisions. Clinically relevant actionable mutations were identified for each patient through this comprehensive genetic profiling and defined as tier 1 variants according to the European Society of Medical Oncology Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (ESMO-ESCAT) classifications and the joint guidelines of the Associated of Molecular Pathology (AMP), ASCO, and College of American Pathologists (CAP).7,8
Genetic Testing Methods
Comprehensive genomic profiling used the FoundationOne Liquid Companion Diagnostic (F1LCDx) assay (Foundation Medicine Inc, Cambridge, MA). F1LCDx, a hybrid capture–based NGS in vitro diagnostic device, detects genomic alterations in over 300 cancer-related genes using circulating cell-free DNA from patients' plasma (Data Supplement, Table S1).
Tissue-based genetic testing in the standard-of-care clinical setting at NTUH included EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and BRAF mutation analysis (Data Supplement, Table S1). EGFR mutation testing was performed using Roche cobas EGFR Mutation Test V2 (EGFR cobas V2). ALK was detected by immunohistochemistry (IHC) with the Ventana anti-ALK (D5F3) antibody. ROS1 rearrangement was screened by IHC using anti-ROS1 IHC clones, SP384 (Ventana, Tucson, AZ) or D4D6 (Cell Signaling, Danvers, MA), and confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization, or reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. BRAF mutation was detected through anti-BRAF V600E monoclonal VE1 antibody for IHC, and confirmed by cobas BRAF V600 mutation test. Optional tissue NGS such as FoundationOne or ACT genomics was available commercially.
Data and Statistical Analysis
We performed an analysis to evaluate the concordance of tissue-based genetic testing in the clinical setting and blood-based NGS testing in the trial. The sensitivity of each test was evaluated based on its ability to identify clinically relevant actionable mutations for each patient, including blood-based NGS, tissue EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and BRAF gene testing, and optional tissue NGS. Kappa test gauged agreement between diagnostic methods. A nondetected result from one test indicates that the alternative genetic testing methods identified clinically relevant actionable mutations. To identify the risk factors for nondetected blood-based NGS results, we performed logistic regression analysis to determine independent risk factors. Co-occurring genomic mutations from ctDNA NGS were correlated with clinical outcomes. Progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the time from first dose of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) treatment through the date of radiologically defined disease progression or death. Overall survival (OS) measured the time from the start of systemic cancer treatment to death or the last follow-up on June 30, 2022. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The log-rank test was used to compare survival between groups. Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were used to adjust for potentially interacting covariates and determine the factors associated with PFS and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 22.00 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, IL). P < .05 indicated significance.
RESULTS
Patients' Characteristics
From February 2019 to March 2022, a total of 274 patients at NTUH received blood-based NGS ctDNA assay at cancer diagnosis. Five of them had samples that did not meet the sequencing quality control metrics for computational analysis. Finally, 269 patients (98.2%) with the F1LCDx assay yielding results were included, of whom 264 also underwent tissue-based genetic testing and 20 patients had tissue NGS (Data Supplement, Fig S1). Median age was 64.9 years. Most of the patients were diagnosed with adenocarcinoma (87.4%). Additionally, 245 (91%) patients had stage IV disease and 80 (29.7%) presented with baseline brain metastasis. Table 1 displays characteristics of all patients.
TABLE 1.
Actionable Mutation Landscapes
Clinically relevant actionable mutations (ASCO/AMP/CAP and ESMO-ESCAT tier 1 variant) were identified in 205 (76%) patients after comprehensive genetic profiling by both clinical tissue and BFAST liquid testing (Fig 1A). Females and nonsmokers demonstrated a significantly higher percentage of actionable mutations than males and ever-smokers (86.1% v 65.9% by sex, 89.7% v 54.8% by smoking; P < .05, chi-squared test, Table 1). Seven of 16 patients with squamous cell carcinoma also had actionable mutations. EGFR mutations were detected in 138 (51%) patients. Of these mutations, 47(34%) were exon 19 deletions, 65 (47%) were L858R, and 17 (12%) were exon 20 insertions. Rare mutations, such as ALK, ROS1, RET, BRAF, KRAS, ErbB2, and MET were found in 7, 8, 1, 10, 20, 15, and 6 patients, respectively, with a prevalence ranging from 0.4% to 7% in our cohort (Data Supplement, Table S2).
The prevalence and distribution of uncommon or complex EGFR mutations were revealed through blood-based NGS of 101 patients with EGFR mutation. Compound mutation accounted for 9.7% of the EGFR-mutated cases. No exon 19 deletion combined with other mutations were detected in our cohort. Six patients (5.3%) with L858R compound mutation were identified (Fig 1B).
Diagnostic Accuracy of Blood-Based NGS
Concordance Between F1LCDx and Tumor Tissue Clinical Genetic Testing
Concordance data for F1LCDx and tissue genetic testing are shown in Table 2. Tissue-based genetic testing identified 144 (53.5%) patients with clinically relevant actionable mutations and did not detect known driver alterations in 61 (22.7%) patients, with a sensitivity of 70.24%. Of these 144 patients, 138 were detected by standard-of-care genetic testing and the other six were found by optional tissue NGS. By contrast, liquid NGS identified clinically relevant actionable mutations in 171 patients and failed to detect mutations in 34 (12.6%) patients, resulting in a sensitivity of 83.41%. Mutation outcomes for various methods are provided in the Data Supplement (Table S3). With the complementary use of ctDNA NGS testing, the number of patients detected with clinically relevant actionable mutations increased from 144 to 205, representing a 42% increase in the detection rate. The performance of diagnostic methods by mutation subtypes is provided in Figure 1C.
TABLE 2.
Concordance Between F1LCDx and EGFR cobas V2
We had 138 patients with EGFR mutations in our cohort, of whom 121 showed mutations other than exon 20 insertion. EGFR cobas V2 failed to detect mutations in 13 patients. The undetected mutations included 2, 7, 1, 1, 1, and 1 case(s) of exon 19 deletion (L747_P753delinsS and E746_A750del), L858R, L861Q, L833V/H835L, L747P, and V765M, respectively. The concordance rate and Cohen's kappa coefficient were 88.5% and 0.76, respectively (95% CI, 0.68 to 0.84, substantial agreement; Data Supplement, Table S4).
Seventeen patients had EGFR exon 20 insertions. Among this population, the concordance rate between the F1LCDx assay and the EGFR cobas V2 was 96.3%, and Cohen's kappa coefficient was 0.53 (95% CI, 0.27 to 0.78, moderate agreement; Data Supplement, Table S5). EGFR cobas V2 identified 10 of the 17 patients (58.8%) with EGFR exon 20 insertion. The mutations not detected by the EGFR cobas V2 included 3, 1, 1, 1, and 1 case(s) of EGFR-A763_Y764insFQEA, EGFR-N771_P772insAH, EGFR-P772_H773ins NPNP, EGFR-H773_V774insPH, and EGFR-H773>PYNPY, respectively. Underdiagnosis of EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation variants could be concerning while using EGFR Cobas V2 for EGFR mutation diagnostic assay.
Factors for Discordant Blood-Based NGS ctDNA Results
Thirty-four (12.6%) patients went undetected using F1LCDx assay. Upon univariate analysis, the predictors associated with nondetected blood-based NGS ctDNA results included age (odds ratio [OR], 1.49 [95% CI, 1.08 to 2.04; P = .014), tumor (T) stage (OR, 0.31 [95% CI, 0.15 to 0.66]; P = .002), node stage (OR, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.17 to 0.78]; P = .009), metastasis (M) stage (OR, 0.16 [95% CI, 0.07 to 0.37]; P < .001), no brain metastases (OR, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.10 to 0.74]; P = .011), and no bone metastases (OR, 0.14 [95% CI, 0.05 to 0.38]; P < .001). Elderly, lower stages, and absence of brain or bone metastases showed difficulty in detection of results. Further multiple logistic regression model demonstrated that lower T (OR, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.15 to 0.79]; P = .012) and M (OR, 0.21 [95% CI, 0.09 to 0.49]; P < .001) stages significantly correlated with the nondetected F1LCDx results (Table 3). The results elucidated that nondetected F1LCDx assay results could be attributed to lower or lack of ctDNA shedding.

Co-Occurring Genomic Alterations
Co-Occurring Mutations' Landscapes
Along with the clinically relevant actionable mutations, 123 other co-occurring mutations were found in the BFAST NTUH cohort. TP53 (54.3%), DNMT3A (30.1%), TET2 (12.3%), CTNNB1 (6.7%), PIK3CA (6.3%), and RB1 (6.3%) were the most common co-occurring mutations from blood-based NGS ctDNA assay (Fig 2A). Figure 2B illustrates the distribution of these actionable and common co-occurring mutations.
Co-Occurring Genomic Alterations and Clinical Outcomes
The limited cases with mutations, such as ALK, ROS1, RET, and MET, hindered clinical outcome correlation. We exclusively examined patients with EGFR mutations for co-occurring mutations and survival outcomes. The most frequently occurring mutations, including TP53, DNMT3A, PIK3CA, TET2, CTNNB1, RB1, and DNA repair genes, were included in the analysis.
Among the patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC, 54, 25, and 35 patients received first-generation, second-generation, and third-generation TKIs, respectively. First-generation compared with third-generation TKI use (hazard ratio [HR], 0.50 [95% CI, 0.26 to 0.96]; P = .04) and the presence of PIK3CA mutation (HR, 2.03 [95% CI, 1.00 to 4.12]; P = .05) were significantly associated with a shorter PFS under EGFR-TKIs in the univariate analysis. TET2 (HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 0.96 to 3.60]; P = .06) and RB1 (HR, 2.13 [95% CI, 0.85 to 5.34]; P = .11) showed potential significance and were included in the multivariate analysis. However, in the multivariate analysis, only first-generation compared with third-generation TKI use (HR, 0.43 [95% CI, 0.22 to 0.86]; P = .02) and co-occurring TET2 mutations (HR, 2.49 [95% CI, 1.22 to 5.10]; P = .01) remained significantly associated with shorter PFS of EGFR-TKI treatment (Table 4 and Data Supplement, Fig S2). We categorized the patients according to the generation of TKI received. The correlation between TET2 mutation and EGFR-TKI remained evident in the first/second-generation TKI group but not in the third-generation TKI group. However, the median PFS was not reached in the third-generation TKI group, likely because of inadequate follow-up time (Data Supplement, Fig S3). No co-occurring mutations were found to be related to the OS. Disease stage was the only factor associated with OS in the patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC (Data Supplement, Table S6).

DISCUSSION
We present the results of BFAST Taiwan cohort study, including the concordance between tissue-based clinical gene testing and blood-based NGS testing, Asian population's oncogenic landscape, and co-occurring mutations. We also assessed the performance of F1LCDx and the limitations of EGFR cobas V2 in detecting EGFR mutations.
Our study used comprehensive genetic testing and found oncogenic driver mutations in around 76% of Asian NSCLC cases. By contrast, in Western populations, driver oncogenes were reported in only 38%-61% of the cases.9,10 The previously reported incidence of oncogenic mutations in the Asian population (68%-84%) was similar to our study.10-12 This disparity in driver mutations was largely attributed to the contrasting prevalence of EGFR mutations. EGFR mutations were identified in up to 50% of the cases in Asian populations but only in 10%-16% of Caucasians.13 These findings highlight the importance of thoroughly searching for druggable mutations in Asians to improve treatment outcomes.
The comprehensive ctDNA test has been reported to have a high positive concordance with tissue-based genotyping and the potential to increase the detection rate of actionable oncogenes by 45%-75%.1,9,14,15 Similarly, with the complementary use of ctDNA NGS testing, the detection rate of actionable mutations increased by 42% in this study. The major reasons for failure to detect mutations in the standard-of-care clinical practice could be the following: First, every single-gene testing method had its limitations. EGFR cobas V2 had a 14.5% nondetected rate in our study. ROS1 IHC detected only 75% of ROS1-mutated lung cancers in our cohort. Six of the seven patients (85.7%) with BRAF V600E mutation were positive for VE1 IHC, while other BRAF mutations, such as G469X, were not identifiable by the VE1 IHC test. Furthermore, RET, KRAS, ERBB2, and MET were beyond the scope of current standard-of-care genetic testing in the clinical settings at our institution, making NGS the only method to detect these oncogenic mutations.
Our study revealed that the EGFR cobas V2 had a nondetected rate of 10.7% in EGFR mutations excluding exon 20 insertion and 41.2% in EGFR exon 20 insertions. Previous reports indicate that commercially available PCR kit methods may miss over 50% of exon 20 insertion.16,17 The EGFR cobas v2 is a real-time PCR test that specifically targets certain variants in the EGFR gene. However, the sensitivity of such hotspot panel tests reduces if other nontargeted variants are present in the gene. The cobas system mainly fails because of primer limitations in the hotspot analysis. Three patients in our study had rare EGFR mutations (L833V/H835L, L747P, and V765M) undetected by EGFR cobas V2 but identified by the F1LCDx assay. Unlike cobas, NGS comprehensively analyzes more genomic regions, detecting a wider range of alterations. The performance of EGFR cobas v2 has been validated for use with both formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue and plasma samples.18-23 However, real-world use might be affected by factors such as biopsy specimen quality and quantity, affecting testing success.24,25 A previous study reported that the false-negative rate of EGFR cobas test could increase up to 50% when the tumor content was <10%.26 Some classical mutations within the coverage of the predesigned primers in the EGFR cobas v2 were also missed by the test in our cohort, including 1, 7, and 1 patients each with exon 19 deletion, L858R, and L861Q, respectively. The tissue content and quality could be attributed to the nondetected results. Notably, three patients in our cohort had the A763_Y764insFQEA mutation, accounting for 17% of exon 20 insertions. This mutation is located within the C-helix of EGFR and responds to first- to third-generation EGFR-TKI.27-29 However, the EGFR cobas v2 hotspot analysis cannot detect this mutation owing to limitations in the primer design. Although the frequency of A763_Y764insFQEA mutation is typically reported to be around 5%-8% of exon 20 insertions, our study found a higher prevalence.30-33 With the increasing use of NGS in clinical practice, gaining information about the actual prevalence of rare mutations might be possible.
In our study, the F1LCDx assay had a nondetection rate of 16.6%, which could be attributed to the variability in the shed rate of tumor DNA into the bloodstream.1,34 We observed that approximately 32% and 21.9% of the patients with M1a and M1b with driver mutations, respectively, showed negative results in the ctDNA analysis. However, the nondetection rate decreased to 3% in M1c patients. Extrapulmonary metastases have been associated with positive plasma tumor ctDNA,5,35 whereas isolated brain metastases showed lower ctDNA levels.36 Our study confirmed the link between extrathoracic metastases and ctDNA shedding. In our cohort, there were a total of 80 patients with brain metastases. Only 19 of them had isolated brain metastases. Most of patients had multiple organ metastases in addition to brain metastases. This may account for the correlation of brain metastases with positive liquid biopsy results in univariate analysis.
Co-occurring mutations in PI3KCA and CTNNB1 are notably enriched in EGFR-mutant cancers, influencing EGFR p.Thr790Met occurrence and EGFR-TKI response.37 Similarly, the activation of the PI3K pathway has been linked to decreased response in BRAF V600E-mutant NSCLC targeted therapy.38 These mutations were identified in our EGFR-mutated cohort at frequencies of 6.3% and 6.7% similar to previous study.
Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) variants have been identified as a possible cause of false positives in the ctDNA analysis.39,40 Older age and previous exposure to radiotherapy or chemotherapy increased the chances of detecting CH mutations.41-43 The use of higher sequencing depth and targeted sequencing is attributed to an increased detection rate of CH mutations.41 Our study population consisted of treatment-naïve individuals, which reduced the influence of treatment-related CH mutations. However, age and detection methods could still cause misclassification of CH mutations as tumor mutations. Two meta-analyses revealed that the co-occurrence of TP53 mutations had negative impacts on prognosis and was linked to unfavorable outcomes under EGFR-TKIs.44,45 However, our study did not show any association between co-occurring TP53 mutations and survival. The possibility of TP53, also recognized as a common CH mutation, interfering with the interpretation of prognostic biomarker analysis cannot be ruled out.40,46,47 Instead, the association of TET2, another age-linked CH mutation, with PFS under EGFR-TKIs was noted in our cohort.48,49 Upon adjusting the age factors in the multivariable analysis, the association persisted. TET2 loss-of-function mutations are known to associated with DNA hypermethylation and tumor progression, and implicated in the development of both hematologic and solid cancers.50,51 Additionally, TET2-mutated immune cells derived from CH have been shown to affect the cancer microenvironment and worsen solid cancer development.52 The observed association between TET2 mutations and PFS under EGFR-TKIs may be attributed to either intrinsic tumorigenesis in lung cancer cells with TET2 mutations or CH-driven immune microenvironment changes. Further investigation is needed to clarify the mechanism.
Our study has certain limitations. Although we discussed the diagnostic accuracy of ctDNA genetic testing, it should be noted that no gold standard currently exists for identifying genomic alterations. Additionally, tissue NGS was considered optional in our cohort, and only a portion of the patients underwent tissue NGS. Furthermore, nontumor CH mutations may result in the misinterpretation of ctDNA results, especially the co-occurring mutations. Finally, the number of patients with rare mutations, such as RET, MET, ROS1, and ALK, was limited, which limited the possibility of analyzing co-occurring mutations in those groups.
In conclusion, NGS ctDNA analysis is clinically valuable for molecular testing, offering more convenience and completeness than conventional tissue-based genotyping in NSCLC. By complementing tissue-based genotyping with ctDNA NGS testing, the detection rate of oncogenic mutations increases by 42%. However, limited ctDNA shedding in lower-stage patients poses challenges for blood-based NGS ctDNA assays. Our study suggests that co-occurring mutations such as TET2 affect EGFR-TKI treatment duration; however, the influence of ctDNA-detected CH mutation is currently unclear.
